Messages.Author: pd...@lightlink.com
Messages.Body:
So in a particularly preposterous game we just played involving 4 vote
decks, we had an inordinate amount of title contestation--at one point
in the game, we had 2 Princes of Atlanta contesting, 2 Princes of
Boston contesting, 3 Princes of DC contesting, and then we noticed that
we also had an Archbishop of DC in play too. We became confused and
looked in the newest rulebook, and discovered that according to the
ambigious wording, a given city can have one Prince or Archbishop,
which made us more confused, and then we remembered the old obsolete
Sabbat rule about vampires getting to fight 'cause of this sort of
thing, and got even more confused.

So what happens if there is a Prince and an Archbishop of the same city
in play at the same time? Do they contest?

Thanks,
-Peter

Messages.Author: brokenstep
Messages.Body:
> So what happens if there is a Prince and an Archbishop of the same city
> in play at the same time? Do they contest?

Yes.

Messages.Author: Daneel
Messages.Body:



Yes, they do. Just out of curiousity I looked up the relevant piece of
text. Much to my surprise, I found nothing on the C,R,E page, even
though I distinctly recall when this was "errataed" after SW came out.
Oh well, the rulebook says (4.2, first paragraph):

Some titles are unique. For example, there can be only one prince or
archbishop of a particular city (see Vampiric Sects, sec. 10). If more
than one vampire in play claims the same title, then the title is
contested. While the title is being contested, the vampires involved
in the contest are treated as if they have no title, but they remain
controlled and may act and block as normal.

I guess the devil lies in the details. I can see though why you would
get the impression that princes and archbishops contest among
themselves, but not among eachother... I guess if many people draw
the same conclusion, it would be better to elaborate the concept of
city-based dominion (and say something like, some titles are tied to
and represent dominion over a given city - irrespective of the actual
title (Prince, Archbishop, Baron or Monitor) vampires reigning over
the same city are considered to contest).

--
Bye,

Daneel

Messages.Author: James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In message <ops2m1yd...@news.chello.hu>, Daneel <dan...@eposta.hu>
writes:

>I guess the devil lies in the details. I can see though why you would
> get the impression that princes and archbishops contest among
> themselves, but not among eachother... I guess if many people draw
> the same conclusion, it would be better to elaborate the concept of
> city-based dominion (and say something like, some titles are tied to
> and represent dominion over a given city - irrespective of the actual
> title (Prince, Archbishop, Baron or Monitor) vampires reigning over
> the same city are considered to contest).

This is actually sort-of already done, but in 10.x rather than 4.x.
10.x is much more explicit about this, and is referenced by 4.x which
only mentions it as an example.

10.1 The title of prince is associated with a particular city
and can be contested by another vampire who claims the title of
prince or archbishop of the same city.

10.2 Like Camarilla princes, the title of archbishop is
associated with a particular city and can be contested by
another vampire who claims the title of prince or archbishop of
the same city.

These ever-so-slightly unhelpfully gloss over Barons, which is covered
only in 10.5.

10.5 The title of baron is associated with a particular city
and can be contested by another vampire who claims the title of
prince, archbishop or baron of the same city. If the title is
contested with a prince or an archbishop, then the anarch's cost
to contest it is increased by 1 blood.

--
James Coupe

Messages.Author: pd...@lightlink.com
Messages.Body:
Daneel wrote:
> I guess the devil lies in the details. I can see though why you would
> get the impression that princes and archbishops contest among
> themselves, but not among eachother.

Yeah, I think when Sabbat came out, the titles didn't contest each
other (i.e. you could have both a Prince and an Archbishop of the same
city), but there was that wacky "they can attack each other" rule,
which may have always been optional, but then quickly became disavowed
by the inherriting design team.

It seems reasonable that when the rules were refitted with the WW
takeover, the Prince/Archbishop rules were reconsidered or clarified,
and I never noticed. As noted, that Princes and Archbishops (and
Barons, for that matter) all contest each other isn't spelled out in
the same portion of the rules as the rules for title contestation
(section 10 vs section 4?), so it is easy to miss. At least by me.

And as I can't remember the last time I was in a game where we had
contested titles, let alone a 4 way contestation between 3 Princes and
an Archbishop, I haven't really thought about it till now :-)

-Peter

Messages.Author: Brent Ross
James Coupe
Messages.Body:
In message <dpkrdu$qhh$1...@rumours.uwaterloo.ca>, Brent Ross

<bwr...@csclub.uwaterloo.ca> writes:
>Actually, the net sum of the way these are worded is that
>contesting titles is asymmetric. A baron can have his title
>contested by a prince or archbishop without contesting their
>title at all (since they are explicited listed as only contesting
>each other). With the extra cost when contested this seems
>really bad for barons, and I'm having a hard time believing
>this is whats really intended... especially since section 4.x
>doesn't handle barons at all, which suggests that this is a
>huge oversight in need of rewrite.

Going backwards:

4.x isn't in need of a rewrite. 4.x says:

4.2. Contested Titles

Some titles are unique. For example, there can be only one
prince or archbishop of a particular city (see Vampiric Sects,
sec. 10).

It also doesn't mention Justicars, or the card-text based title of
Liaison, either. The example is just that - an example.

Regarding the wording, it is slightly awkward but the effect is not what
you describe.

10.5 The title of baron is associated with a particular city

and can be contested by another vampire who claims the title of

prince, archbishop or baron of the same city. If the title is

contested with a prince or an archbishop, then the anarch's cost

to contest it is increased by 1 blood.

It doesn't really matter who kicks off the contesting in the first
place, as once a title is contested (such as a Prince contesting a Fee
Stake) it applies to both (or more) holders of the title - they contest
each other. So it doesn't matter if it's the Prince who starts it or
the Baron (or the Archbishop).



But your arguments seem to be based on the idea that 'contesting' is
where one vampire is paying blood while they don't have the benefit of
their title. But contesting, by it's very nature, requires two or more
vampires to be contesting amongst each other. The idea that the Baron
has his title inert and paying for it, while the prince or archbishop
who shares his city does not, is meaningless. That's not contesting,
that's one vampire squirting blood out it's anus for no reason.
